directAnswer: Pope John XIV, born Pietro Canepanova, was bishop of Pavia and imperial chancellor for Italy before Emperor Otto II arranged his election in late 983. After Otto's sudden death, the antipope Boniface VII returned, imprisoned John in the Castel Sant'Angelo, and he died there in August 984.

sections.h2: Otto II's Chancellor and Bishop of Pavia
paras: Pietro Canepanova came from Pavia, the old Lombard capital, and served as its bishop. He was also Otto II's archchancellor for Italy, one of the emperor's most trusted administrators. When Benedict VII died in 983, Otto, then in Rome, secured Pietro's election. He took the name John, by most accounts out of reluctance to bear the name of the apostle Peter as pope.
Because he was chosen by the emperor rather than through the usual Roman process, the local nobility regarded him as an outsider.

Within weeks of John's election, Otto II died in Rome on 7 December 983, still in his twenties. The emperor was buried in the atrium of St. Peter's. The heir, Otto III, was a small child in Germany, leaving the pope without effective support in a hostile city.

In April 984 the antipope Boniface VII, who had been in Constantinople since his flight a decade earlier, came back to Rome with the help of local allies. He had John seized and imprisoned in the Castel Sant'Angelo. John died there on 20 August 984, according to the sources either from starvation or by poison. Boniface held the city until his own death the following year.

keyFacts: Born Pietro Canepanova in Pavia; bishop of Pavia
Archchancellor of Italy under Emperor Otto II
Chose the name John rather than reign as Peter
Imprisoned by antipope Boniface VII; died in the Castel Sant'Angelo

faqs.question: Why didn't Pope John XIV keep his baptismal name?
faqs.answer: His name was Peter, and he chose John instead, by most accounts out of reverence for St. Peter, whose name no pope had taken as a papal name.

faqs.question: How did John XIV die?
faqs.answer: He was imprisoned by the antipope Boniface VII and died in the Castel Sant'Angelo in August 984, reportedly of starvation or poison.
